Semantic Works: Tea Time Planner: Episode 1: The Afternoon Tea

Tea Time Planner:
Episode 1: The Afternoon Tea

A planning app for a real British afternoon tea for seven, with a 3D table, sandwich recipes, a drinks table and a day-by-day plan, built while Pasha and Olga planned the party out loud. Built by Pasha and Claude in 1 hour 27 minutes, 100% by voice: no code or commands entered by keyboard.

0:00 – 0:02 · Requests 1 – 2

It started with "Hello, Olga!" and a party to plan

Pasha and Olga were hosting a British afternoon tea for seven, and Olga would be doing the cooking. Pasha asked for an empty page first, to watch while he talked:

New project. Start a local Python server and build an HTML page that says "Hello, World!" and "Hello, Olga!". I'll just watch that page and talk to you, so push all your changes to the page.Pasha, to Claude

Then he began describing the party:

I'll narrate the facts of our tea party for seven people, all girls, and as I do, draw a picture of the table with everything we discuss. … Start with the table and the two tea containers; I'll be watching the page.Pasha, to Claude, lightly trimmed

There was no specification and no mockup. The app grew one spoken request at a time, while the decisions about food, tableware and timing were still being made.

The build · 0:00 – 1:27

Then came the build: 79 requests in 87 minutes, in seven phases

Many of Pasha's requests were questions about the party itself: which bread, which spread for the roast beef, where to buy clotted cream in Tampa. Each answer went onto the page as a decision, a recipe or a shopping item. Looking back, the build had seven phases.

  1. The table takes shape (0:00 – 0:04): an oval, then a rectangle, then three on each side and one at the head.
  2. Sandwiches and the first 3D plate (0:05 – 0:16): five kinds of finger sandwich, and three views to switch between.
  3. A real app layout (0:19 – 0:30): full screen with a side panel, flip-card recipes, the bread and the timing.
  4. The 3D British table (0:31 – 0:38): each place set the British way, two tall stands, candles, a slow turn.
  5. Keeping a record (0:38 – 0:45): the transcript, screenshots taken by themselves, cameras that survive a reload.
  6. The plan (0:48 – 1:18): a checklist for the day, filters for the cook and the helper, shopping by store.
  7. Polish (1:19 – 1:27): the title and colours, 3D drinks with steam and bubbles, curved chairs.
The build · phase 1 of 7 · 0:01 – 0:04 · Requests 2 – 4

Phase 1: we drew the table as Pasha described it

From the first description, Claude drew the table from above with a teacup at each place and the two glass teapots in the middle, and kept a running list beside it: guests, teaware, teas, and a first shopping list.

  • An oval first, with seven seats: the shape had not been said yet.
  • Then a rectangle, two minutes later, with the seats corrected twice while Pasha talked it through with Olga.
  • Two teas in two glass teapots: African Nectar, which they had, and Palais des Thés.
Correction: three seats on each long side and one at the head.Pasha, to Claude
The build · phase 2 of 7 · 0:05 – 0:16 · Requests 5 – 12

Phase 2: we put the sandwiches on a 3D plate, with three views

Food was the worry: Olga had no helpers and had to make everything. Pasha listed the sandwiches they were sure of, asked what goes with roast beef, and asked for views.

View 2, food: only the sandwiches, each shown open and assembled; better, draw them on a plate I can rotate with the mouse.Pasha, to Claude
  • Four platters on the table, then three views behind one button: the table, the food, the drinks.
  • A 3D plate of finger sandwiches that turns with the mouse: smoked salmon, egg and salmon, shrimp and crab, roast beef with horseradish cream, and a fifth, chicken.
  • Answers became the page: garnishes for each kind, how to cut fingers, where to find scones and clotted cream.
The build · phase 3 of 7 · 0:19 – 0:30 · Requests 13 – 20

Phase 3: we gave it a real app layout and recipe cards

  • Full screen, nothing scrolls: the view on the left; on the right a side panel of sections that open and close, which slides in and out and can be resized by dragging.
  • Gold buttons top right: one to switch views, one to hide the panel. The page remembers what was open.
  • Flip-card recipes: each sandwich has a card in the panel; click it and it turns over to short steps, with the garnish last.
  • Bread and timing: a thin-sliced square loaf, as in Britain, and a schedule so the bread does not go soggy.
  • The fifth sandwich changed three times: coronation chicken, a salad of roasted thighs, then chicken Waldorf from a rotisserie chicken.
When I see a sandwich, I can click it and it flips like a card: brief cooking instructions, garnishes included, on the back.Pasha, to Claude
The build · phase 4 of 7 · 0:31 – 0:37 · Requests 21 – 24

Phase 4: we set the table in 3D, the British way

Lay out plates, cups, knives and forks the way they do in Britain … Draw it in 3D, like the sandwiches, so I can turn and zoom the whole table.Pasha, to Claude, lightly trimmed
  • Each place: a tea plate with a white napkin, fork on the left, a small knife on the right, cup and saucer above it.
  • Camera buttons: Angle, Top and Seated, a switch to hide the guests, and the flat plan kept as a second drawing.
  • Fixed along the way: the first showing stopped half drawn. The code used a shape this version of three.js, the 3D library, does not have. Simpler shapes fixed it within minutes.
The build · phase 4 of 7 · 0:32 – 0:44 · Requests 22 – 25, 34

Phase 4, continued: stands, candles and a slow turn

Pasha told Claude what they had already bought, and the table was laid out again to match.

  • Down the middle, mirrored: a bouquet, a tall three-tier stand, jam and clotted cream, the two teapots with milk, sugar and lemon, then the same again.
  • Floating candles in glass cylinders, with pearls inside them under the water, and a few at their base.
  • A slow turn: one round in about two minutes, tipping between a high view and a lower one, never under the table.
  • The saucers were there but white on white; a gold rim made them show.
Animate the 3D table, slowly, like the sandwich plate turns, and only from attractive angles: never under the table.Pasha, to Claude
The build · phase 5 of 7 · 0:38 – 0:45 · Requests 26 – 35

Phase 5: we kept a record of how it was made

  • A transcript of the conversation, timed from Pasha's first message. The first ways of asking for it were stopped by an automatic safety check; asked again more plainly, it went through.
  • Screenshots that take themselves: a few seconds after each change, the server photographs every view in a hidden browser and keeps the ones that changed, numbered and timed. 115 in all.
  • The earlier steps were collected from the screenshots Claude had taken while checking its work.
  • Cameras remembered: each live update used to reset the 3D views. Now each camera keeps its angle, zoom and spin, and an update lands without a jump.
Put the screenshots in a subfolder called screenshots, numbered 1 to n, with a timeline saying when each was made, so I can map them to the transcript.Pasha, to Claude
The build · phase 6 of 7 · 0:48 – 1:18 · Requests 36 – 68

Phase 6: we turned the decisions into a plan for the day, for the cook and the helper

  • A fourth view, Plan: the day before and the party day, for a 6:30 PM start, as a checklist with ticks that are remembered; with music and small gift ideas.
  • One shopping list per store, with tickboxes: Amazon, Publix, Whole Foods, Sam's Club, Walmart, then what to check at home. Each side-panel section belongs to one view.
  • Olga · main cook, Pasha · helper: a name pill on every step, and filters for Everyone, Olga, Pasha, and Together for the steps that need both.
  • Moved to the day before whatever could be: flowers, setting the table, the candles, Pasha's AI art on the TV. An hour to get ready at 4:00, with a nap for Olga only.
  • Fixed along the way: the header buttons stopped responding in Pasha's window, until they were moved a little lower; and splitting the list by store deleted part of the page's script, which was restored from Claude Code's saved history of the file.
The build · phase 7 of 7 · 1:19 – 1:26 · Requests 69 – 77

Phase 7: we polished the title, the colours and the buttons

  • A title: "Semantic Works: Tea Party for 7".
  • One line under each view, centred: what it shows, and "drag to rotate · scroll to zoom".
  • Cream for every view, and in Plan each day as a white sheet of paper, like a printout.
  • Buttons centred across the view: the camera buttons on Table, the filters on Plan.
  • Gold section headings in the side panel, with the five sandwich names in bold black so they stand out.
Background colours: Drinks and Plan have a white main view, but Table and Food are cream. …Pasha, to Claude, lightly trimmed
The build · phase 7 of 7 · 1:22 – 1:27 · Requests 73, 75

Phase 7, continued: 3D drinks with steam and bubbles, and curved chairs

Let's animate the Drinks view and make it 3D.Pasha, to Claude
  • A round side table with a white cloth, turning slowly like the others.
  • The two glass teapots with steam rising from the lids; two red and two white bottles; a Coke.
  • Champagne in an ice bucket, and two flutes with bubbles rising.
The chairs at the table: the back comes up to table height, and it's curved.Pasha, to Claude

The chairs were redrawn with a low curved back, level with the table top. The last request was a question about the sandwiches, answered on the page: cream cheese on both slices, edge to edge, to keep the bread dry.

The result

A planner for one afternoon tea, from the table to the shopping

One page with four views, each with its own side panel. Deployed as one HTML page and one script, with three.js for the 3D and a small Python server for live reload and screenshots. Built by Pasha by voice: no code or commands entered by keyboard.

TableA 3D British tea table that turns by itself, with camera presets and a flat plan.
Each placeA flip card showing how to set it, then seven short steps.
Food15 finger sandwiches of five kinds on a 3D plate.
RecipesA card per sandwich that flips to its recipe and garnish.
DrinksA 3D side table with steam from the teapots and bubbles in the flutes.
PlanA checklist for the day before and the party day, with ticks.
Cook and helperFilters for Everyone, Olga, Pasha and Together.
ShoppingOne list per store, with tickboxes.
MemoryTicks, open sections, flipped cards and cameras survive a reload.
Its own record115 screenshots on the same clock as the transcript.

0:00 – 1:27 · The whole conversation

What it took in tokens

Counted from the session's own log: 60 million tokens across 225 requests to the model, all Claude Opus 5.5, from Pasha's first message to the end of the transcript.

KindTokensWhat it is
Re-read from cache59,372,879The conversation so far, read again on every request. This is 99.0% of the total and is billed at a small fraction of the normal rate.
New input332,150Text entering the conversation for the first time: Pasha's messages, tool results, files and screenshots (450 plain, 331,700 written to the cache).
Output273,309Everything Claude wrote: answers, code, commands and its working notes.
Total59,978,338

The total is large because of how a long conversation works, not because much was written. Each of the 225 requests re-reads everything before it, so the same text is counted again and again: on average about 264,000 tokens of history per request. Not included: the work after the transcript closes, such as writing this journey.

What that would cost in dollars

About $20 on Claude Opus 5.5, the model that ran the session. The same token counts priced on another model:

ModelRough costNotes
Claude Opus 5.5about $20.00What we used: $11.87 for cache re-reads, $2.66 for new input, $5.47 for output.
Claude Sonnet 5.5about $15.90The same token counts at Sonnet's prices. Its cache-read price is the same as Opus, so the saving is small.

Caching is what keeps this small. With no caching, every re-read would be billed as fresh input: about $244 on Opus 5.5.

  • A pricing comparison, not a prediction. Another model would take a different number of steps to do the same work.
  • One assumption: cache writes priced at the one-hour rate, twice the input price.
  • Prices as of October 2026, Anthropic's pay-as-you-go prices per million tokens: Opus 5.5 $4 input, $8 cache write, $0.20 cache read, $20 output; Sonnet 5.5 $2, $4, $0.20 and $10. The same ones used on the other Semantic Works journeys.
Open

What is not done

  • Still open at the end of the session: which wine is already in the fridge; lobster meat for the shrimp salad, only if it can be found; ready-sliced bread or a bakery Pullman; the shopping trip for the teapots and dessert knives; the party date, allergies, exact quantities and which small gift.
  • Not checked: what the stores have in stock. Claude said so each time; the page tells you to call ahead.
  • One party only. The sandwiches, the plan and the shopping list are written into the page; another party means changing it by voice again.
  • One browser only. The ticks are kept in the browser that made them, so Olga's phone and Pasha's do not share them.
  • No tests. Everything was checked by looking at it.
  • It needs the internet when run on its own, to load three.js from a public CDN. The copy in this presentation carries its own.

The conversation that built the page, with Pasha's requests as understood, is in TRANSCRIPT.md; the 115 screenshots and their timeline are in screenshots/.
